sets.title: How two towns built a bridge
sets.summary: Students read a local history narrative about two towns building a bridge and practice finding facts, sequencing events, explaining causes and identifying the author's purpose.

passage.title: The Willow Bridge
paragraphs: Long ago, two small towns sat on opposite sides of the Gray River. Willow Bend was on the north side, and Stonefield was on the south side. Families in both towns were farmers, and they often traded food and tools. But there was one big problem: there was no bridge.

To cross the river, people had to ride a small wooden ferry. The ferry could carry only six people at a time. In the spring, heavy rain made the river fast and dangerous. Sometimes the ferry could not cross for many days, and farmers could not sell their vegetables before they spoiled.

In 1898, a teacher named Rosa Delgado had an idea. She asked both towns to work together and build a bridge. At first, many people said it would cost too much. Rosa collected a few coins from every family. She also asked carpenters and blacksmiths to give their time instead of money.

Building the bridge took two years. Workers cut logs from the forest and carried stones from the hills. Children brought water and lunch to the workers. In the winter, the work stopped because the ground was frozen. When spring came, the workers started again.

In 1900, the Willow Bridge finally opened. People from both towns walked across it together and held a large festival on the riverbank. Trade between the towns grew quickly. Today, a new steel bridge stands in the same place, but a small sign still tells Rosa's story.

sets.title: Colors and heat from the sun
sets.summary: Students read about a class experiment with colored jars and practice using data, explaining cause and effect with absorb and reflect, and evaluating why a test is fair.

passage.title: The Color Test
paragraphs: On a sunny afternoon, Kofi noticed that his black backpack felt hot, but his friend's white backpack felt cool. He wondered if color changes how much heat an object takes in from the sun. His class decided to test the question.

The students filled three jars with the same amount of cold water. They wrapped one jar in black paper, one in white paper and one in silver foil. They put a thermometer in each jar and placed all three jars in the same sunny spot on the playground.

Every 15 minutes, the students checked the thermometers and recorded the temperature. At the start, the water in every jar was 15 degrees Celsius. After one hour, the water in the black jar was 27 degrees, the white jar was 20 degrees, and the silver jar was 18 degrees.

Their teacher, Ms. Lindqvist, explained the results. Sunlight carries energy. Dark colors absorb most of the light that hits them, and that energy turns into heat. Light colors and shiny surfaces reflect much of the light away, so they warm up more slowly.

The class used what they learned. They suggested painting the roof of the school shed white to keep the tools inside cooler in summer. Kofi decided to wear lighter colors on hot days, too, and he now keeps his black backpack in the shade.

choices.why: The teacher explains that dark colors absorb light and the energy becomes heat.

choices.why: 3 degrees is how much the silver jar warmed, not the difference.
choices.misconception: Uses only one part of the comparison

choices.why: This compares the black jar with the white jar, not the silver jar.
choices.misconception: Uses data from the wrong jar

choices.why: The black jar warmed 12 degrees and the silver jar warmed 3 degrees, so the difference is 9.

choices.why: When everything else is the same, the students can tell that color caused the change.

choices.misconception: Adds information that is not in the text

choices.why: The water got warmer in every jar, and the test was meant to measure that.

sets.title: A plan for a book swap
sets.summary: Students read a student council notice that gives directions and argues for a book swap, and practice following steps, finding main ideas and judging evidence.

passage.title: Student Council Notice: Start a Book Swap!
paragraphs: Dear students and families, the Student Council of Lakeview Elementary has a proposal. We want to start a book swap in the front hallway. A book swap is a shelf where you can leave a book you have finished and take a different one home for free.

Why do we need a book swap? Last month, we asked 120 students about reading at home. In our survey, 84 students said they want more books at home. Many students also said they have books they have already read many times. A swap would let those books find new readers instead of sitting on a shelf.
A book swap is also good for the planet. When we share books, fewer books end up in the trash. Families can save money, too, because new books can be expensive.

Here is how it will work. First, bring a book that is in good condition, with no torn pages. Next, give it to a council member at the hallway table on Monday or Wednesday morning. Then, choose one book from the shelf to take home. Remember: one book in, one book out.

Some people worry that the shelf will get messy. To solve this problem, two council members will check and organize the shelf every Friday. Please vote yes for the book swap at the class meeting on May 3. Together, we can share the joy of reading!

items.stem: Which detail gives the strongest evidence that students want a book swap?

choices.why: This answers a worry, but it does not show what students want.
choices.misconception: Picks a true detail that does not support the claim

choices.text: 84 of 120 students said they want more books.
choices.why: This number comes from asking students, so it shows many of them want more books.

choices.text: New books can be expensive.
choices.why: This is a reason for families, not proof of what students want.
choices.misconception: Chooses a reason instead of evidence for the specific claim
